claims.statement: X documents an API Key and Secret (also known as Consumer Key and Secret) as credentials of an X developer App; the secret is the second half of that pair, shown once when the App is created, and regenerable from the Keys and tokens tab.

sources.supports: The API Key and Secret (also known as Consumer Key and Secret) are the most fundamental credentials required to access the X API.
Please note that we only display these credentials once, so make sure to save them in your password manager or somewhere secure.
sources.locator: How to acquire an API Key and Secret

claims.statement: X states the consumer key and secret are used to sign OAuth 1.0a requests or generate user tokens, and that they should be treated as sensitive as passwords.

sources.supports: Authenticate with OAuth 1.0a. Used to sign requests or generate user tokens.
These values should be considered as sensitive as passwords, and must not be shared or distributed to untrusted parties.

claims.statement: X's Creating a signature page documents the consumer secret as a secret input: when the token secret is not yet known, the signing key is the percent-encoded consumer secret followed by an ampersand, and otherwise the consumer secret and the OAuth token secret are combined into the signing key. The oauth_signature is the base64 form of the HMAC-SHA1 output of the signature base string and signing key, a derived output that is not the consumer secret. The oauth_consumer_key is listed among the request parameters in the signature base string; the page does not call it public or secret.

sources.supports: In this case, the signing key should consist of the percent encoded consumer secret followed by an ampersand character ‘&’.
Finally, the signature is calculated by passing the signature base string and signing key to the HMAC-SHA1 hashing algorithm.
Both of these values need to be combined to form a signing key which will be used to generate the signature.

claims.statement: The worked example on X's Creating a signature page uses an example consumer key of 22 characters, an example consumer secret of 43 characters and an example OAuth token secret of 41 characters, all letters and digits, in a request whose oauth_timestamp (1318622958) falls in October 2011. The page presents them as example values and states no length or alphabet for issued values, so these lengths describe the example only and are not a format statement. The values are not copied here.

sources.supports: Table rows for oauth_consumer_key, Consumer secret and OAuth token secret in the worked example (values not copied).

claims.statement: Gitleaks (rule twitter-api-secret) and TruffleHog (twitterconsumerkey detector), maintained separately, both capture exactly 50 letters and digits as the Twitter API key secret, each beside a 25-character key and each gated on a twitter-related context word. This records consistency of those two artifacts at the pinned commits; it is not a provider statement, and neither artifact states the period or app type its length describes.

sources.supports: Rule twitter-api-secret captures 50 alphanumeric characters after a twitter keyword; rule twitter-api-key captures 25.
The consumer key detector captures 25 alphanumeric characters as the key and 50 as the secret.

claims.statement: One rule artifact, Nosey Parker rule np.twitter.2 (Twitter Secret Key), captures 35 to 44 letters and digits after a twitter-related context word with key or secret words; its pattern is generic across secret-like values, so it is not scoped to the consumer secret. No second artifact states this range, so it is a lead and not a corroborated claim.

sources.supports: Rule np.twitter.2 (Twitter Secret Key) captures 35 to 44 alphanumeric characters; rule np.twitter.1 captures 18 to 25 for the identifier.

claims.statement: Scanner rule artifacts disagree on the length of the X API Key Secret (50 in two artifacts; 35 to 44 in one), and the provider's worked example (43 characters, a 2011-dated request) is inside the second range and outside the first. No X page read states the length of an issued consumer secret or whether it changed over time, so the length is unresolved and no structure is recorded; neither figure is chosen, and no union range is recorded.

sources.supports: Rule twitter-api-secret captures 50 alphanumeric characters after a twitter keyword; rule twitter-api-key captures 25.

notes: Project-authored by the Redact Secret project, which maintains this repository; not independent evidence. Draft; not yet reviewed. Revision 2 supersedes revision 1 additively. It splits the two-versus-one length evidence into a corroborated 50-character claim (two maintainers), a single-artifact 35-to-44 lead and the unresolved conflict, adds the provider's secret-input and signature-output roles and the provider example's lengths, and records no structure because no provider statement gives the length of an issued secret.

openQuestions.question: Whether the 35-to-44 versus 50 character difference reflects an older and a newer issuance, different credential kinds matched by a generic rule (a consumer secret and an access token secret), or rule imprecision is not stated by any official page read. An X statement of the length history with dates, or a dated archive snapshot of an X page that states a length, would settle it. An issued sample would be issuance-gated and was not sought. No sample value from the artifacts was copied.

Whether the API Key (consumer key) is documented as a public identifier or as confidential is not stated; the pages call the pair credentials and compare them to a username and password, and the signature page lists oauth_consumer_key among request parameters.

The OAuth token secret (access token secret) is a separate credential in the same signing key (family x:oauth1-access-token-secret); its length, as shown by the 41-character provider example and the generic Nosey Parker pattern, is not shown to differ from the consumer secret by any page read. A bare value of either kind is not attributable to one of them by shape.

The signing key uses the percent-encoded consumer secret. Whether an issued secret can contain characters that percent-encoding changes (so the encoded and raw forms differ) is not stated; the examples read are letters and digits only.
